title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
claim: Two distinct goals call for two distinct restarts at a known change point, each optimal for its own criterion and not the other's.
layout: Top decision tree flowing into two boxes, with two log-log plots below
description: The top half is a flowchart. A box reading 'Break announced in advance' splits with dark arrows into two question boxes. The left box asks 'Will the next interval cover?' (conformal reliability) and the right box asks 'Was the miss rate on target?' (frequency calibration over a finished period). Each question has a colored arrow to a method box: pink 'Restarted quantile' with 'best attainable rate', and orange 'Restarted ACI' with 'a faster rate'. The bottom half has two log-log line plots against the number of forecasts since the break. Panel a shows the reliability gap. The pink restarted quantile line falls with slope −0.499, while ACI (blue dashed) and restarted ACI (orange) flatten at about 0.078 and 0.065. Panel b shows the frequency gap. Restarted ACI falls fastest (slope −1.004), ACI follows (−0.994), and restarted quantile is slowest (−0.574). Direct labels with bold slopes sit at the right of each plot. The pink and orange colors link the boxes to the plot lines.
caption: An announced break admits two restarts, and each attains the rate of one criterion and misses the other's. The second row of boxes asks what the forecaster needs, coverage of the next interval or a finished period's miss rate on target. Against the number $m$ of forecasts since a simulated mean shift, panel a plots the reliability gap, the expected distance of the next interval's coverage from nominal coverage, and panel b the frequency gap, the miss rate's distance from its target.
abstract: A prediction interval should contain the outcome at a stated rate. Conformal prediction sets its width from past forecast errors. When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, intervals set from errors before that break can stop covering. After Australia moved to five minute electricity settlement, a 90% interval fixed beforehand covered 51.5% of the next 400 days. One forecaster needs the next interval to cover, another a finished period's share of misses at 10%. We show that each need calls for its own restart at the date. We recompute the next interval from the $n$ errors since the break. If these errors are independent, its coverage comes within $O(n^{-1/2})$ of the stated rate, the best order attainable. For a finished period, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI). On bounded errors, if a floor under its width adds a bounded total, it brings the share of misses within $O(n^{-1})$ of target but promises nothing about the next interval. After a simulated mean shift of 5.0 noise standard deviations, recomputed intervals cover within 3.5 percentage points of 90% on average at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five baselines. Of nine announced breaks in power markets and at a central bank, restarting ACI gives a detectable gain only at the one large break.
